overview: Democrats won majorities in both the House and the Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections, according to Wikipedia's news summary, and President Trump replaced chief of staff Susie Wiles with adviser Stephen Miller, the AP and CBS reported. Global stocks fell sharply this week as investors questioned heavy spending on artificial intelligence, while the October jobs report came in stronger than forecast. Abroad, bomb threats diverted flights across Europe, and New Zealand voted in a general election.

stories.headline: Trump names Stephen Miller White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
stories.summary: President Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller, his top immigration adviser, will become White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. The move came days after Republicans lost the midterms. Democrats criticized the pick, and Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican, said Trump should rethink it.
stories.why_it_matters: The chief of staff runs the White House and shapes what the president hears, so this choice signals how the administration plans to deal with a Democratic-led Congress, including on immigration policy.
stories.background: Susie Wiles became the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff when Trump returned to office. Stephen Miller has been a close Trump adviser for years and is known as the main architect of the administration's immigration crackdown. The change follows midterm elections in which Democrats won the House majority, per the coverage. Tillis is a Republican senator from North Carolina who has criticized Trump advisers before.

facts.text: Trump confirmed that Wiles will step down and Miller will replace her; Trump said 'I wanted to make a change.'
Miller has led the administration's immigration and mass-deportation policies and has been their public face.
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) called Miller 'the worst of all possible choices' and said Trump 'needs to rethink' the decision.
Democratic lawmakers criticized the appointment, using terms such as 'hatemonger' and 'xenophobe', per the Guardian.
The Hill reported the pick sets up a contentious two years with the incoming Democratic House majority.

framing.note: Ties the change to the GOP's midterm defeat in the headline.
Uses Trump's own explanation and the word 'installs'; plays down the reaction.

stories.headline: Mississippi Senate race between Hyde-Smith and Colom still undecided
stories.summary: Days after the midterms, Democrat Scott Colom and Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith remain separated by a razor-thin margin, with provisional and mail ballots still being reported. Lawyers for both campaigns are preparing for a possible legal fight. Mississippi has no automatic statewide recount.
stories.why_it_matters: Control of a Senate seat in a state Democrats haven't won since 1982 hangs on a handful of ballots, and the dispute over voter rolls and ballot counting could affect who gets to vote and how quickly results are certified.
stories.background: Hyde-Smith is the Republican incumbent in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator since 1982. Colom, a Democratic prosecutor, mounted a competitive challenge, and independent Ty Pinkins also ran. Mississippi's counting of provisional ballots is slow and decentralized, per NPR. Early-count reports put the two within tens of votes.

facts.text: The NYT and CBS reported Colom held a slim lead as more provisional and mail ballots were reported.
NPR reported that no one knows how many ballots are still outstanding, and described Mississippi's process as among the slowest and most decentralized in the country.
Axios reported scrutiny of a voter-roll cleanup after some voters said they had problems casting ballots.
The BBC reported that lawyers for both campaigns are preparing for a possible legal battle.
Ty Pinkins told CNBC he aimed to boost Colom's vote and avoided campaigning in heavily Black areas.
Mississippi has no automatic or candidate-initiated statewide recount law, per Democracy Docket.

framing.note: Calls the race 'still a toss-up' while noting the Democrat's slim lead.
Focuses on voter-roll problems rather than the horse race.
Frames it as an upset threat, stressing how unlikely Colom's run looked beforehand.

stories.headline: Senior Justice Department officials resign, including head of 'grand conspiracy' probe office
stories.summary: Jason Reding Quiñones, U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, resigned, the second senior Justice Department departure since the midterms. stories.headline: US carries out new limited strikes on Iran as Tehran weighs mediators' proposals
stories.summary: President Trump said the US military carried out a new round of what he called minor strikes on Iran on Friday, aimed at an air defense system. Iranian media reported explosions on Qeshm Island near the Strait of Hormuz. Separately, officials said Iran is reviewing mediators' proposals that touch on its nuclear program.
stories.why_it_matters: The fighting and the threat to shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz can affect oil prices and the safety of commercial shipping. A deal on the nuclear program and the strait would be a step toward ending the conflict.
stories.background: The US and Iran are in an active conflict that has centered on Iran's nuclear program and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for oil. Qatar is the lead mediator, and earlier proposals have included reopening the strait in stages alongside nuclear talks. Iran has long refused to discuss parts of its nuclear program, which is why reports that it is now reviewing proposals on the subject stand out. Earlier this week a prior US attack on Iran was made public, and voters' views of the war were part of coverage of the US midterm elections.

facts.text: Trump said the US military carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran on Friday, targeting an air defense system, and described them as minor.
Iranian state media reported two explosions on Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz; Tasnim news agency said two missiles struck the island.

Officials told several outlets Iran is reviewing proposals focused on its nuclear program; The Hindu cited regional officials as saying mediators and Iran have discussed a possible bridge deal to pave the way for further talks.
A diplomat told The Japan Times that Tehran is showing willingness to discuss nuclear issues that were previously off the table.
A Greek-owned tanker, the Velos Sapphire, was struck in the Gulf on Nov. 5 and a seafarer was killed, according to the ship's operator; Iran said two other vessels were on fire.
The Guardian reported that Qatar is trying to persuade Tehran to let UN nuclear inspectors visit bombed nuclear sites, and that the Strait of Hormuz could reopen as part of that plan.

stories.headline: Russian missiles hit Kyiv and energy sites ahead of talks in Abu Dhabi
stories.summary: Russia struck Kyiv and the surrounding region with missiles and drones overnight, hitting energy facilities and a major bridge, according to Ukrainian authorities. At least one person was reported killed and several wounded. Ukraine is preparing for new talks with Russia and the US.
stories.why_it_matters: Strikes on power and fuel infrastructure affect heating and electricity for civilians heading into winter. The talks could shape whether the fighting slows.
stories.background: Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 and the war has continued since, with Russia repeatedly targeting Ukrainian power and gas infrastructure. Ukraine has struck back at Russian oil facilities. Outlets say Russia recently stepped up air strikes. The US has been involved in diplomacy, and the latest round of trilateral talks with Russia and the US is expected in Abu Dhabi.

stories.headline: Wave of hoax bomb threats hits European flights and Irish newsrooms
stories.summary: At least 20 flights in Europe received hoax bomb threats within hours, and several newsrooms in Ireland were evacuated after false threats. The Irish government said it appears to be a coordinated campaign. European security agencies are reportedly examining whether the threats originated in Russia.
stories.why_it_matters: Travelers may face diversions and delays, and aviation authorities say any change in procedures will take a long time.
stories.background: Hoax bomb threats against airlines are not new, but officials and experts describe this wave as unusual in volume and timing. The threats have been sent by email to airlines and media organizations. They come amid other security incidents in Europe, including a cyberattack on supermarket refrigeration systems reported by The New York Times. European governments have been urging public resilience and stockpiling.

facts.text: At least 20 European flights dealt with bomb threats within hours, and one expert told CBS the pattern suggests 'a very deliberate act'.
Ireland said the threats to Irish media outlets and European airlines are probably part of a coordinated campaign.
The Financial Times reported that European security agencies are probing whether the hoaxes started in Russia, with a working hypothesis of pro-Kremlin activists or hacking groups.
CNBC reported that analysts see in-flight targeting as aviation's weakest point and that procedure changes would be slow.

stories.headline: Paraguay's Senate removes President Peña over Ueno Bank collapse; he is placed under house arrest
stories.summary: Paraguay's Senate removed President Santiago Peña on Friday over the collapse of Ueno Bank, which left millions of customers unable to reach their money. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president. Outlets report Peña was then placed under house arrest on suspicion of breach of trust.
stories.why_it_matters: Frozen accounts, pension funds and health care funds affect ordinary Paraguayans directly. The case tests how the country handles a banking failure tied to its government.
stories.background: Ueno Bank, a digital bank, was seized by regulators earlier this week, freezing customer accounts. Peña was a shareholder in the bank's parent company until 2025, according to AP-based reporting, and the central bank chief he appointed resigned at his request. Protesters gathered outside Congress and opposition lawmakers pursued impeachment. Peña offered to resign, but lawmakers went ahead with the process, which removes protections former presidents enjoy.

stories.headline: Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu cleared of treason, sentenced to four years for incitement
stories.summary: A Tanzanian court on Friday acquitted opposition leader Tundu Lissu of treason but sentenced him to four years in prison for incitement. The conviction relates to statements before the October 2025 presidential election. Avoiding a treason conviction means he avoided a possible death sentence.
stories.why_it_matters: The case is a gauge of political freedom and the treatment of opposition figures in Tanzania after a disputed election.
stories.background: Lissu leads the opposition and has been detained since April last year, according to the BBC. His treason trial followed Tanzania's disputed presidential election in October 2025 and a deadly crackdown on protests. He says the charges are politically motivated.

facts.text: The court acquitted Lissu of treason, finding prosecutors had not proven he intended to intimidate the government, and sentenced him to four years for inciting people to disrupt last year's election.
Lissu has been detained since April last year and says the charges are politically motivated.
Lissu condemned the incitement conviction, which he said was not among the charges he faced, according to DW via AllAfrica.
The election was disputed and followed by a deadly crackdown, RFI reported.

stories.summary: Airstrikes on a market in al-Waziyah in Yemen's Taiz province killed at least 30 people and wounded 15, according to a Houthi health ministry spokesperson. The Houthis blamed Saudi airstrikes, while government forces and local authorities disputed that.

stories.headline: Global stocks fall as AI shares sell off after Democrats win Congress
stories.summary: US technology stocks fell sharply on Thursday, with the Nasdaq entering a correction, and the losses spread to Asian and European markets on Friday. Outlets tie the move to doubts about heavy AI spending and to fears that a Democratic Congress will curb data-center growth. US stocks partly recovered Friday, with the Nasdaq up and the Dow slightly lower.
stories.why_it_matters: Many 401(k)s and index funds are heavily weighted toward the big tech and AI companies, so a drop in those shares can show up directly in retirement balances. If the AI spending slowdown continues, it could also weigh on corporate investment and hiring.
stories.background: Over the past two years, a few large technology companies and AI developers have driven much of the stock market's gains, spending heavily on chips and data centers. Questions about whether that spending will pay off had been building for months. Data centers also became a campaign issue because of their effect on local electricity bills. Democrats won control of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, and investors began pricing in more regulation and oversight of AI and big tech.

CBS News said the Thursday rout was driven by concerns about a possible slowdown in data-center construction and pushed the Nasdaq into a correction.
Bloomberg put the week's global losses at $5.7 trillion; The Guardian said Apple, Tesla and Nvidia together shed about $1 trillion in one session.
The Wall Street Journal reported US stocks ended Friday mixed after strong jobs data and a modest AI rebound that did not settle investor nerves.
Reuters, as carried by The Star (Malaysia), reported data-center stocks fell and renewable-energy shares rose after the Democratic sweep.
OpenAI's CFO told CNBC the company will keep expanding its data centers despite the election result.
The Wall Street Journal reported stock-picking hedge funds unwound positions last month at the fastest rate in over a decade.

stories.headline: US employers add 165,000 jobs in October, well above forecasts
stories.summary: The Labor Department said employers added 165,000 jobs in October and the unemployment rate slipped to 4.1%. Economists had expected far fewer jobs. The Financial Times said the data reinforces expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates.
stories.why_it_matters: A stronger job market is good for workers, but it can keep the Fed from cutting rates, which affects mortgage, car-loan and credit-card costs.
stories.background: The monthly jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics is one of the main gauges of the US economy. The Federal Reserve has a dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices, so hiring and inflation data shape its rate decisions. Markets have been jumpy about the economy this week because of the AI-stock sell-off, which made the report more closely watched than usual.

markets.summary: Wall Street had a rough week. Tech stocks fell hard on Thursday, with the Nasdaq slipping into a correction (a drop of 10% or more from a recent high), and the selloff spread to Asia and Europe on Friday. Coverage in the Guardian, Deutsche Welle and the Financial Times tied the move to doubts about huge AI investments and to investor worries about how a Democratic Congress might treat the sector. Bloomberg put the week's losses at about $5.7 trillion. Stocks steadied somewhat on Friday after the Labor Department reported that employers added 165,000 jobs in October, well above the roughly 59,000 analysts expected, and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%. The FT noted that strong hiring reinforces expectations the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates, which is another pressure on richly priced stocks.

concept.explanation: It is the government's monthly count of how many jobs employers added, excluding farms, and it comes out on the first Friday of most months. It moves with business confidence and hiring demand, and markets watch it because strong job growth can keep the Fed from cutting interest rates, or push it toward raising them. That matters to your wallet because the Fed's rate decisions feed through to mortgage, car and credit card rates, and a surprise in either direction can swing stock prices that sit inside most retirement accounts.
